Mu. ALFRED WALTON is no doubt sincere
in all he writes, and I believe him to have the
best intentions towards the working classes,
but I am persuaded he is wrong in his facts.
Is it, or is it not, the fact that the landlords,
as a class, let their land at." enormous"
rents'? I have known Lincolnshire, Notting-

for forty years or more, and lam confident
, that the tenants themselves would tell Mx.
WALTON that in those districts he is quite
mistaken. I see no yeason why the landlords
in these three counties should be, more just,,
ruoro liberal, or more sensible than landlords
in Wiltshire, Dorsetshire, or Devonshire. I
know nothing about the rents in Warwick-
shire, where the labourers are striking, and per-
baps Mr. WALTON knows as little, but I gave
the labourers' own account of their employers'
position, in opposition to Mr. WALTON'S, and
they must be much better authority. It is
admitted by experienced and well-informed
persons that a tenant ought, to have nearly, if
if not quite, £lO an acre capital to
stock his farm and manage it properly.
It is true he may, what is called, "get into a
farm with less, and la great industry increase
gradually his capital. On. reading Mr.
WA.l.Tores paper carefully , over, I must ad-
, mitin onenense he may be right in describing
the rents in his district as "enormous." He
,says the majority of the tenant farmers would
have a hard struggle to raise 5,000 shillings
instead of 5,000 pounds to farm 500 acres
of land. Now ten shillings an acre is an
enormous rent for a man to pay who has only
ton shillings an acre capital to farm it with.
A man with XS or £lO an acre would prosper
.at three times the rent, and he would do so by
employing far more labour in cultivation.
I farmed 300 mires of land for eleven years at
a far, higher rent than is paid in the South and
West of England, and. I got very good interest
for my capital. I once had a crop of beans
a second time over, at 4s. 6d. an acre, and I
had exactly a sack of beans an acre extra,
which sold for a guinea-400 per cent. profit in
about three mouths. I have never seen the
districts' to which Mr. WAraorr alludes, but I
_am quite sure that no landlord can obtain an
, enormous rent for more than three or four

not be paid. Whatever the rent may be that
these struggling tenants are paying with only
a tenth part of the capital they ought to have,

the very great advantage of the labourer, and
the nation at large. speal‘in geizOrally,

the great fault of many landlords is

THE "QUARTERLY REVIEW"

VERSUS THE WORKING CLASSES.

SINCE my last letter on this subject, a friend
has drawn my attention to a silly article in
one of the silly monthlies entitled "Slashing
style," wishing rue to show that when
Albermarle-strect,
charged Mr. MURRAX, of
Nith•having prostituted his quarterly to pro-
Inulgate a deliberate falsehood to the injury of
the working classes, that not only was I fully
'justified in doing so, but that suoh a charge
made in a distinct manner was far better for
object which I wished to obtain than any
roundabout terms, such as "M'. Merrily was
mstaken," or " Mr. Murray had forgotten,"
or any of the numerous phrases which might
have wrapped up the fact that, Mr. MURRAY
had stated a deliberate falsehood, and had also
iopted the " +/pp s io Veri" to - such au

extent as enabled him to conceal a fact which
would have shown to all who read the article
the deliberate falsehood of which he had. been
guilty.
As a matter of course, all men who indulge
in doing wrong when it suits their purpose
(and no one is so thoroughly debased as to do
wrong far the pleasure it affords) hate this

"slashing style," and do all in their power to
render it disliked, except the legitiiiiate one
of reforming their own conduct, and, thank
GOD, there have always been men in this
country who do not hesitate to use the
" slashing style" when the occasion requires
it, careless of the hatred of those who use
enormous lying; or, still more contemptible,
equivocation, in which the PREMIER is such a
proficient.

There is no doubt that lying is not an
English vice, and that, as a rule, our nobility,
as well as the working class, hate all lying,
and scorn the liar. Although the fact cannot
be doubted that there is more than one dis-
graceful exception at present in the House of
Lords, but coneisting of men, principally
laWyers, who have been pitohforked there. It
is especially a middle-class vice, and although
far from believing in POPE'S celebrated line,
"A tradesman thou, and hope to go to heaven."
Yet there is little doubt that the practice
of daily exaggerating the value of what
they sell, and unduly depreciating that
which they buy, is not favourable to vera-
city, yet :when they 'rise in society they are
so conscious of their former habit, that
they, as a rule, carefully abstain from
lying. A member of Parliament detected in
a deliberate falsehood would be immediately
denounced, while the promoter of a swindling
oonipany is coniidered 'olever fellOw if he
succeeds in floating his abomination, throwing
the loss upon others, and he is only denounced
as a swindler when he fails anti is ruined-.

Of course none of Mr. MIJIMAY's customers
belong to the working class; and, therefore,
he could not injure himself or his business,
however much he injured them by his delibe-
rate falsehood, but he might benefit himself
by pandering to the personal profit of all

who benefit their pockets by keeping things as
they are; and verily their name is legion, con.
'listing as a rule of all the Directors of the
Bank of England, and other rich men.
If Mr. MURRAY pleads ignorance of the
subject, or forgetful of the facts which he
cannot deny, but which, as the question now
stands, he is proved to have wilfully concealed
with the view of preventing his readers from
detecting his deliberate falsehood, and Will
apologise to you as the organ of the working
°lasses, he will hear no more on the point,
except my advice not to write upon a subject
of which he is ignorant, and which deeply effects
the interests of others, and a recommendation
that he should read the pamphlet entitled,
" Necessity of altering our Monetary Laws,
proved from the Highest Monetary Authorities."

IT would be well if all the parties to a dis-

In my humble opinion he is alike ignorant

"

without' the prat:o4l(M' of aii; open court and
jury Arial. But, one of our gravest charges

stantiating the matter of the information,"

MIRE OF CARTERS.
On Monday the strike of the Liverpool carters,
which has been for some days apprehended, coin.

menced, when about 6,000 men abstained from
work. The differences between the men and their

employers relate both to matters of time and wages.
Hitherto the hours of the men have been long and
indefinite, sometimes extending as far as 16 and 18
hours per day. The men seek to limit the time of
work to 12 hours per day of actual work with
carts and horses, exclusive of some two or three
hours employment at the stables, and to be paid
for overtime at the rate of 6d per hour. The
masters, on the other hand, desire to fix the time
of working with the carts and horses at 11 hours
per day, instead of limiting it to 12 hours; and
they are then willing tq pay for overtime at the
rate demanded. In respect to the question of time,
the men would probably concede an hour, so that
the difference between them and the masters upon
this pint would be limited to one hour. The
men, however also demand an incretuie of wages
from 275. week, to 30s. The masters meet this
demand half way, and offer 28s. ad. per week. A
minor matter in dispute, that relating to Sunday
work, has been fully conceded by the masters, who
are willing to accede to the wish of the men to
make the number of their visits to the stables on
Sunday two instead of three. The strike,, on
Monday extended from the "quay carters" (or
those who cut goods to and from warehouses) to
the general carriers' men, whose employers are
forwarding agents throughout the kingdom and
whose business lies a good deal in the carting of
goods to and from the railways. Thu e the only
large carters able to conduct their business in
Liverpool on Monday were the railway companies.
The result has been a pretty general suspension of
business throughout the docks and warehouses,
causing immense inconvenience and loss to many
merchants and shipowners. Should the strike
continue, the dispatch of several ships and steamers
must necessarily be postponed; or the alternative
must be adopted of sending them off with their
cargoes short-shipped. During the day a small
number of the masters conceded the demands of
the men, and Mr. Simpson is endeavouring to bring
about an arrangement between the merchants and
the master carters, whereby the latter are to
receive higher rates from the former, so that they
in turn may be enabled to make some concessions to
the men. The maaters, at present, state that their
great difficulty in mooting the men arises from the
Net that, the merchants are in the habit of deduct-
ing a discount frem their accounts, and that the
war4ousemen have to receive curtain gratuities or
fees, which all tend to diminish their profit upon
the cartage. Some members of the masters'
committee are now in the agricultural districts in
search of men as substitutes for those on strike.
Tirousoax.—The strike among the carters in
Liverpool continues, notwithstanding that the
Mayor has used all his influence, in conjunction
with the President of the Chamber of Commerce
'and several influential members, to bring it to a
close. In consequence of the determination of the
men to hold out, and the refusal of the new hands
brought into Liverpool by the agents of the Liver-
pool Cartermen's Association from the agricultural
districts to work at lcs wages than the men now
on strike, there is a most serious derangement in
the loading and unloading of vessels in dock. The
wean-going and. coasting steamers have in several

• different stations in the time permitted by the
faro bill; and as the carters employed by the

held a meeting on Holbeek Moor in the evening,
when they recommendei those who remained out
to resume or obtain work as best they could. There
was a large attendance of men, women, and. girls,
who walked to the Moor accompanied by the Leeds
model band. The various speakers addressed the
meeting from a waggon. Mr. ,W. Kendell, chair-
man of the Flax Operatives Committee, occupied
the chair.

The chairman said that they had now dwindled
down to very few in number. He believed that if
all the men who originally came out had remained
on strike, as they ought to have done, they would
have obtained sufficient support from the outside
publics to have provided for all the women, girls,
and men who came out. Whilst men who had
abandoned the very standard they assisted to raise
wore daily returning to work, the committee
thought that there was little on no use in protract-
ing the struggle.
Mr. Morris, Beeston-hill, who has acted as
secretary throughout the movement, read the
correspondence between the masters and the asso-
ciation, extracts from which have already appeared.
Mr. Wrigley, a member of the Engineers' Asso-
ciation, in addressing the meeting, said he enter-
tained strong hopes that Mr. Mundella would
not lose sight of the movement. .They must en-
deavour by petitions and other influences to
support leaders like Mr. Mundella, who would
look after their interests. Nor should they lose
sight of the promoters and leaders of their asso-
ciation. It was the intention of many outside
supporters of the strike to form a joint committee,
bold
.a meeting early in the week, and place the
principal officers of the association in a position
beyond the reach of poVerty. (Cheers.)
Mr. Luke Hope moved, and Mr. Paul seconded,
a vat° of thanks to the mechanies generally, for the
manner in which they had supported the struggle.
The resolution was passed with acclamation, and
the meeting terminated.

BRADFORD.

PItOP06111) DENIONSTILATION OF TIIADB UNIONISTS.

, It has bean resolved, at a meeting of delegates
representing about 2,600 members of tradois *ode-

ties in Bradford, to hold a demonstration consist-
ing of a procession and out-door meeting, on
Saturday the Bth June, the object being to assist,
as far as possible, :the efforts now being made by
the Parliamentary Committee appointed by the
Trades Congress, held at Nottingham, in January
List, to watch over the interests of trade societies
in Parliament, and advocate, as far as possible, the
the repeal—or such a modification as will give
satisfaction, and remove the clauses that have so
far given cause for the great amount of ill-feeling
that now exists on account of the frivolous prose-
cutions that have taken place—of the Criminal
Law Amendment Act. Attention is also directed
to the bill introduced into Parliament to abolish
the truck system, and the necessity of Govern-
ment being urged to pass the bill.

articles.title: BLACKBURN. STRIEE_ OF WEAVERS.
articles.text:
BLACKBURN.
STRIEE_ OF WEAVERS.

A strike of weavers took place at Messrs. Thos.
Walley and Co.'s, Green Bank Mill, against the
infusion of steam into the weaving shed. During
the week workmen have been engaged in fitting
up perforated pipes for throwing steam into the
shed, and two or three deputations of weavers
waited upon the manager, whole a sou of one of
the proprietors, to protest against the project of
compelling them to work in a cloud of steam all
day long. The hands complained that already
they were suffering severely from having to work
over-sized material, and they urged that, if steam
were infused into the shed, it would not only be
detrimental to their health, but induce the
employers to further over-size their yarns.
They also contend that steaming is un-
necessary, except where the yarns are so over-
sized as to require moisture to enable them to be
woven. The manager refused to listen to the
protestations, and remarked that the firm would
do what they pleased with their own concern.
• During the night steam was forced into the shed,
and at breakfast time Monday morning the
weavers left the mill in a body.

articles.title: SOUTH WALES.
articles.text:
SOUTH WALES.

TUB STEAM COAL TEAM

At the end of January an argument was come
to between the South Wales steam coal colliers
and the masters, by which the then existing atrike
of three months' duration was concluded, an
advance of 12i per cent. being conceded to the
men, and it being arranged that any further rise or
fall that shall occur in the ironworks of Mon•
moutlashire and South Wales shall regulate any
subsequent rise or fall in the arbitration of steam
coal collieries. The recent exceptionally high
prices that have beea realized by steam coals have
already induced the 'men to seek to break away
from this agreement. They now lok that the
basis of tho, wage rate shall be altered and be in-
dependent on the price of steam coal. A meeting
of masters and men was on Thursday held at
Cardiff to discuss the question. Mr. John Nixon
occupied the chair, and most of the principal coal
owners of the district were represented. Twenty-
seven colliers' delegates were present. The pro-
ceedings were conducted with good temper on
both sicles, but theniasters declined to consent to
any alteration of the agreement at present in
force, and pointed out that as yet it had not been
fairly tried. While admitting that steam coals
were now fetching high prices, they pointed out
that the circumstances were very exoeptional,.and
insisted that the general price paid in the district
for cutting coal, &a., was a much more equitable
mode of regulating wages than the fluctuations in
one particular quality of coal could possibly be.
It .is feared that the men will not accept this
decision, in which case another strike with disas-
trous results is to be apprehended.

articles.title: BERLIN.
articles.text:
BERLIN.

TILE LABOUR DISPUTE.

The builders and muter masons of Berlin have
published an announcement stating that, united
with the master carpenters, they had on Saturday
discharged their journeymen in order to oppose the
terrorism and special democratic dictature of the
journeymen. This especially had reference to the
partial strikes against isolated masters, and the
abusive declaration against the masters issued by
the workmen, as well as to prevent the arbitrary
increase of wages and the other concessions, which
were demanded. The announcement calls upon
the public to support them in carrying out their
measures.

HUDDERSFIELD.
TILE CARPENTERS AND JOINERS.

A short time ago the joiners and carpenters of
Huddersfield demanded an advance of 44. a week
and a reduction of 21 houra in the week's work.
The employers refused, and a Court of Arbitration
composed of workme4 an employee, was ap-

pointed to consider the request. After consider-
able discussion the matter ' has been amicably
settled by a compromise—the men are to have 11.
advance instead of 45., and the reduction of hours
that they demanded. The new arrangement takes
effect from the lit of May.

articles.title: STRATFORD-ON-AVON. TllB BUILDING TRADE.
articles.text:
STRATFORD-ON-AVON.
TllB BUILDING TRADE.

The master handers and carpenters met on
Friday evening, at the Red Horse Hotel, to "con-
sider a request on the part of the workmen for a
diminution in the hours of labour and an increase
in the pay. The first was refused, and the second
conceded. A meeting of the journeymen took
place at the Bull's Head Inn, Bull-street, "for
the purpose of considering the best steps to be
taken respecting the nine hours movement." The
result of the deliberations would not be made
known until after the masters had received the
reply of the artisans on Monday.

BIRMINGHAM.

TILE PILE DILICERO.

articles.title: BROMBGROVE. THE CLEPENTERL
articles.text:
BROMBGROVE.
THE CLEPENTERL

The carpenters and joiners employed in the
Midland Company's Wagon Works, at Bromsgrove
Station, are agitating for an inerease of a penny an
hour in their wage, and have addressed a note to
Mr. Harland, the head of the department at Derby,
asking for the increase. As most of the other men
at the works have had an increase of pay, the
parpenters and joiners anticipate a favourable
reply to their request.

YORK.
TUB BUILDING TUADZIL

About two months since a strike took pike
among the journeymen engaged in the building
trades, they requring a reduction of several hours
of work in the week, and to have the same wages
as before. Their employers were willing to meet
them half•way, but their terms were rejected. . In
a beet time, however, the bricklayers resumed
wok on the terms proposed by their employers,
and the same has recently occurred with reference
to the masons, but the joiners still remain out on
strike. It is said that a portion of them have left
York. The proposal of the Masters is 53 hours
per week, at 631 per.hour.

THE CARPENTERS AND JOINERS' STRIKE.

We publish another brief account of the pro-
gress of this strike, this making the ninth week
of the conflict. Some of the masters have con-

articles.title: CLEVELAND. GREAT DEMONSTRATION OF YORKSHIRE IRONSTONE
articles.text:
CLEVELAND.
GREAT DEMONSTRATION OF YORKSHIRE IRONSTONE

MINERS.

On Wednesday a great demonstration of iron-
stone miners of the Cleveland district took place
near Salthurn-by-the-Sea, all the Cleveland
miners being represented. Between 6,000 and
7,000 persons of both sexes, it was computed,
assembled at a mass meeting, which was addressed
by Mr. A. Macdonald, parliamentary agent of the
Miners' Association. The different subjects com-
prised in the programme of the meeting, and
which were discussed, were, shorter hours of
labour, better ventilation of the mines, better
education for the miners' children, the Mines'
Regulation Bill, the Criminal Law Amendment
Bill, and the Servants' Payment of Wages (Truck)
Act. A series of resolutions were passed, fixing
upon eight hours per day as all that was necessary
with the excessive toil to which miners are subject ;
that many of the casualties of the miners are
owing to a want of better ventilation and other
Improved arrangements which the employers
would not supply, and it was decided to ask Mr.
Mundella, M.P., to bring the matter before Parlia-
ment with the view to the appointment of a
Committee of Inquiry by the Government to
ascertain the condition of' the Cleveland miners.
A. better education of the miners' children was
imperatively called for, and the attention of the
Government was called to the fact that a iarge
number of boys worked in the mines without any
• restriction as to age, and that no boys were sent
to school from the mines between ton and twelve
years of age.

articles.title: DERBY. TILE TIIREATENED STRIKE.
articles.text:
DERBY.
TILE TIIREATENED STRIKE.

It has always been my humble opinion that
there are some of the worst, as well as some of the
very best masters in the factories of England; but
that there are more of the former than the latter
is an undeniable fact. In the town of Derby there
are many silk manufactories, where men, women,
and children are employed. The workmen in the
fantories of Nottingham have recently obtained an
advance of 2s. per week—by very strenuous efforts
upon their part—and their fellow workmen at
Derby were determined to have the same advance
if possible. Accordingly they called a meet-
ing together, which unanimously resolved to ask
for the required advance, therefore the different
employers were interviewed, and respectfully asked
for the same advance that had been recently
obtained- at Nottingham, and, As a matter of
course, they refused to grant such an "unreason-
able demand."

The men again called a meeting and as unani-
mously resolved to have the advance—which the
masters would not grant—or at once to send in
their notice papers, which they accordingly have
done, without delay.
Whether this was a rash or somewhat premature
act, I leave you, sir, to judge, as being more com-
petent to form an accurate opinion than I am. The
employers of the differtmt factories at Derby
have also bad a meeting, and determined to lock
out every female employed by them, if the men do
not succumb, and accept what they have previously
"beast satisfied to receive." Such, sir, are the
differences that are continually occurring between
master and man, setting up, as it were, a feud
against each other, a struggle of right and might
for the mastery. But who are in fault I" The
workmen who ash for the reasonable; or the
masters who refuse to grant their request, when
they are getting such enormous profits out of their
workmen's ill-paid labour ?
Who, sir, can tell the serious consequences that
will ensue should the masters take such an
impolitic and unmanly course? We must hope
they • will reconsider their hasty determination,
anklet their employ& receive a small benefit from
the costly work they accomplish so well.

It will not be the men alone that will suffer
should the masters take such au unwise atop—it will

be their families; and moreover, many is the
widowed mother who depends entirely upon her
daughter's earnings for support, for the common
necessaries of life. Such, air, is the manner in
which those masters would compel their work-
people to bend to their wishes, for the sake of the
paltry difference it will be to them. Why should
masters for ever take a pride in seeing their fellow
beings grovelling before them, whilst they
"Make their gold, as if a mine
Had newly sprung, and then combine
Their heaps of wealth to stifle those
That made it. On others woes
To build unrighteous happiness."

What a delightful contrast there is in the man-
agement of Mr. John Smedley's manufactory, Lea
Mills, Matlock, an account of which was described
in your columns of last week.
If there were but more such noble masters as he,
the country would not be so cut up and disunited
with that party spirit which is now so pre-
dominant.

FREDERICK T. IL

CANADA.
THE IJOOKIIINDERS' STRIKE FOR TILE NINE
HOURS.

This question of social reform, which has within
the past few months taken such a firm hold upon
the minds of working men of Canada, is one
which demands full consideration and calm yet
determined action. This curse, it must be
admitted by the unprejudiced and well meaning
portion of the community, has been pursued by
the bookbinders of Toronto. By the course pur-
sued it will be seen that no obstinate dogmatism
has characterised their conduct in the movement
now inaugurated. They feel confident that, by
pursuing the course as stated below, they have
gained the sympathy of all. Surely the sacrifice
made by them commands the support of, every
intelligent working man.
A mass meeting of the working men of Toronto
has been held in the St. Lawrence hail in connec-
tion with the Nino Hours' Movement., Long
before the hour announced for the commencement
of the proceedings, the body of the hall and the
gallery were jammed to the very doors, in fact the
body of the hall was packed with mechanics and
others as thick as herrings in a barrel. A
large number of respectable tradesmen and
others were also present, and it was evident from
the interest which they showed in the proceedings,
that they sympathised with the working men in
the claim which they are now putting for Ward!
The chair was taken at eight o'clock, Mr. j. S.
Williams, President of the Toronto Trade'
Assembly, and the following 'gentlemen were also
on the platform :—Mr. J. Beaty, M.P., Dr. A. A.
Riddel, Aid. Canavan, Mr. E. K. Dodds, Messrs.
A. E. Nugent, President of the Bookbinders
Union ; J. C. McMillan, President of the Toronto
Typographical Union; W. Hewitt, President of
the Coopers' Union ; Richard Nye, Secretary to
It. Hay and Co.'s Employs' Labour Association;
C. E. Tutton, Machinists' and Blacksmiths' Union;
W. Doughtie, Bookbinders' Union ; Messrs. W.
Macgillicuddy, D. Sleith, Bentley, Clarke, andW.
H. Lovell, Typographical Union ; J. Dance, Iron-
moulders' Union; Andrew Scott, Amalgamated
Engineers' Union; M. J. Walker and J. E. Win-
nett, Coachmakers' Union ; Robert MeJennett,
Bakers' Union, and a number of others. '
Mr. Andrew Scott proposed the following resolu-
tion :—" That we the working men of' the city of

Toronto in mass-meeeting assembled approve of
the stand and action taken by the Toronto Typo-
graphical Society and Bookbinders' Union in
coming forward as the pioneers of the nine

hours movement, which they believed must
ultimately prevail throughout the Dominion, and
hereby pledgo them their financial and moral sup!.

port."
Mr. Doughtie, of the bookbinders' union,
seconded the motion. Ho said he was there repre-
senting a small but firmly united body, now on
strike for the fifty-four hours labour per week
system, viz., the bookbinders of this city, to lay
their case briefly before the meeting. On The 17th
January they had mcmoralised their employers to
reduce the working hours, to which they (the
employs) received the usual answer, "that the
application was premature, and that they must
wait a little longer." He thought they had better
wait until the Chinese had it, or wait until the
millenium, and then they would all get it. The
committee referred them to the old country, where
the system bad been n operation for some time.
He concluded by making an appeal to the various
trades to support not only the Typographical
Union but the Bookbinders also.
The resolution WAS carried.

articles.title: MISCELLANEOUS TRADES IkEWS:
articles.text:
MISCELLANEOUS TRADES IkEWS:

SroxE PRIOR.—The strike of fine salt makers
at Stoke Prior Works still continues, though Mr.

Corbett, the proprietor, has used every means to
induce his men to return to work. He has con-
ceded some of their demands, and has promised to
give the full increase asked for as soon as the
state of trade will permit of a rise being made in
the price of salt.
KIDDERMINSTER. —Tho moulders at the Albion
Foundry (Mr. J. Turton's) have struck work.
Mr. Turton agrees with the nine hours movement,
and in fact was one of the first to adopt it. Ile
now wants them to work from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m.,
and they want to work from 6 a.m. to 5 p.m., and
not agreeing on the point they have left their work.
13 IRMING HAIL—The operative bakers resolved
on Thursday night tl come out on strike on
Monday if their demands are not met by the
employers.

DUNDEE.—The saddlers have been conceded a
rise of 3s. weekly, and a reduction of hours to 56.
LANARKSIIIIM.—A meeting of coalminers in
the Glasgow district, held in the Rutherglen Town
Hall on Sunday, decided to compromise their
dispute with the employers. For several weeks
an agitation has been carried on in the district for
an advance of Is. on the day's wages, and an
agreement was come to last week that if the
demand was not conceded a strike would be
resorted to. Meanwhile, several of the employers
offered an increase of 6d, per day, and the men
have agreed to accept the offer "as an instalment."
It is expected that the workmen in the lager mining
districts of Larkhall, Hamilton, and Motherwell,
who have also asked an advance of Is., and have
been offered 6d., will follow the course adopted by
the men in the Glasgow district.
WEARDALE.—The strike of the lead miners in
the employ of Mr. W. B. Beaumont, M.P., is at
an end. The advance of wages on the standard
is 33 per cent, and, taking the abolition of the
per centage system into consideration, the new
arrangements are deemed the most satisfactory

that have been made in the trado. for a great
number of years.

QUESTION.

CONFERENCE IN LONDON.

On Tuesday, the first of two sittings of a Confer-
ence to discuss questions connected with unions
among agricultural labourers was held at Willis's
Rooms.

crests of this country. 2. The regulations of agricul-

'Upwards of a hundred and fifty persons, includ-

more prominent of those present were the Rev.

The Chairman then intimated that letters had

ployer of agricultural labour at Kimbolton, Hunts,
considered the present agitation was alienating

Mr. Arch, Warwickshire labourer, introduced

Sir C. Trevelyan considered the agricultural

peed of a great and most decided improvement in

pose of obtaining an lacrosse of wages :and such

Mr. Young, of Birmingham, considered the

On Saturday last a veryimpmtant meeting was
'held at the Winchester Arms, Southwark-street,
London: The meeting had been convened by
the request
.of Mr. Bass, and was attended by a
large number of the London council, who, how-
ever, were willing that only twelve of their
number should take part in the discussion. Dr.
Langley stated that the London men were ready

.to secure union with
their friends in the provinces. He explained that
the object of the meeting was to discuss the pur-
posed programme for the delegate Meeting in
June, and suggested that Mr. Graham, of Derby,
should tuko the chair without losing auy voting
power. Mr. Graham, having declined, Dr. Baxter

The clauses in the programme were thou dis-

cussed seriatim.
Clause 1. was adopted unanimously..
. .
Clause 2. was altered to read as follows :
"That the Council and officers who have been

government until the delegate meeting shall have
been duly. constituted, arid shall have elected

money contributed for the purposes of the con.
ference from the country diatricts, except the
metreptditan counties; and all district secretaries

scriptions for the conterence to him. Mr. Graham
to report to the chairman of the Executive, Coun-
cil in respect to such contributions.
This amendment and addition was proposed and
seconded by London delegates, and carried unani-
mously.
Clause 3 was altered as follows :
"At the delegate meeting the future rules shall
be first discussed, but, to prevent loss of time, no
proposal in reference thereto shall be entertained
unless notice of such proposition shalt have been
forwarded to the general secretary fourteen days
before such delegate meeting, end every such
proposition 41101 be duly authenticated as having
been approved by ;the vote of a majority of
branch sending a delegate, or as having beeu
approved by, at least, ten members of the society
where a delegate cannot be sent. Such districts,
however, as send their levy for the conference to
Mr. Grail= to remit their propositions through
him to the London executive."

In the course a a very long and animated dis-
cussion on this clause, Mr. (Jaldwell, Manchester
delegate gave an interesting" report of the work
going on in Manchester, and stated that, with a
view to obtain the very best possible code of rules,
they had had a committee of experienced Inell
working hard in the preparation of comprehensive
regulations, based upon the experience of other
societies. Several of the London delegates ex-
pressed their gratification andtheir willingness to
accept any efficient body of rules so prepared. It
NM suggested, moreover, that it would probably
save trouble and expense, if, instead of proposing
independent Tula, the provincial districts would
accept the Manchester rules as the basis of the
future laws. The amended clause was adopted
unanimouoly.
Clause 4 was unanimously agreed to be amended
as follows :
" All branches having fifty members (or united
branches making up that number) to send ,one
representative ; branches exceeding 250 to send
two delegetpa ; exceeding 500, three delegates,
and no more. Delegates unexpectedly prevented
from 'attending may' place their proxies duly
authenticated la the hands of any other delegate.
"Cause 5 was so amended that the credentials
of the delegates in tlAp Metropolitan diltriets were
to be endorsed by Mr. Graham.
"Clause 6 was altered so as to change the date
of the commencement of the delegate meeting from
Jane the lot to 24th, which was unanimously,
agreed to. For Clause 7 the word 'revision' wee
altered to 'consideration,' and words added to the
effect that 'the sitting of the conference on the
first day should eomnience at eleven o'clock
Clause 8 Was adopted, with the exception of the
last senteacereferring to the election of the general
secretary, ha reference to which it was decided that
an advertisement ehotald be published offering
.£250 a year to a gentleman t-inalified to undertake
the duties; that the applications be submitted to
a 110-eennnittee, consisting of Messrs. Piles
(Chester), Caldwell (Manchester), 'Blade:). ("lir-
minghatn), and three members of the Executive
Council, who shall be empowered to reduce the
number by selecting the six most eligible, 'whore
names shall be submitted by lists sent to the
branches through their officers, the gentleman
receiving the moat, votes being elected general
secretary for the ensuingyear.
Clause 10 was amended to read as follows :

"That with 4 view to secure a lair representa-
tion from all parts of the country, the expenses of
each delegate shall be p tid by a levy of one
shilling per member, to be paid into the hands of
the parties authorised to reueive the same (namely,
the general searetary for the llatropolitan districts,
and Mr.Glraham for emtfy distrlots), on or be-
fore the Ibth day `Yune. 'No Member, who has
not paid this nontributibit;,shall be entitled to vote
in 043 ql4gliog a deletutto, and no branch which
hak not pEkia lte levy to the deleipte expellee fund
, ,

on or before t4e 10th pf June shall be entitled to
send a delegate. The allowance to each delegate
to cover such time as may be necessary for him to
come from and return to the branch he represents ;
such allowance to be at the rate of 12s. 6d. a day,
with travelling *wises."
Clauses 11 and 12 were carried unanimously,
without any alteration.
There was at one time the greatest possible
danger of a permanent plit between the metro-
polis and and the provinces, owing to the mis-
representations of certain interested parties, but
mutual explanations and the general spirit of
concession which prevailed on all sides removed
these difficulties. Part of the misunderstanding
arose from the suppression of a letter from the
ehairmau in an organ claiming to represont the
interests of the men, to which the programme had
been sent a fortnight before. Several gentlemen
in the room complained of similar suppressions,
and pointed out that the columns of the journal
referred to were occupied by the Editor's old
communications, which had been in the Dailg
Telegraph some months ago. But the men who
had come together were resolute not to he misled
from the purpose of consolidating the union, and
the meeting broke up with cordial expressions of
good feeling on all sides, and a vote of thanks to
the chairman, who bad sat for nearly seven hours.

Dr. Baxter Langley, accompanied by Mr. George

THE LIBERATION SOCIETY.

The annual meeting of the Society for the
Liberation of Religion from State Patronage
and Control, was held on Wednesday night in
the Surrey Tabernacle, Newington. Mr.
Isaac Holden, of Bradford, occupied the chair.
The attendance was very large.
The Rev. Dr. Laudeis moved the first reso-
lution :

That this meeting regards with the highest
satisfaction the extent to which, at the present
time, the question of disestablishment engages
public attention throughout the kingdom—the
character of the views now expressed by many
influential members of the Establishment, and the
tendency of numerous concurring events to hasten
the approach of the time when the objects aimed
at by this organisation—already partialy effected
—will be completed and finally accomplished,

The Rev. J. G. Boers seconded the reso-
lution, which was carried with acclamation.
The second resolution ran as follows, and
was moved by the Itev. It. W. Dale, of Bir-
mingham, and seconded by Mr. Illingworth,
M.P., and carried :
That looking to the present position of the
question of elementary education in England and
in Scotland, and of University education in Ire-
land—looking also to the antagonism which has
now to be encountered at the hands of the sup-
porters of Church Establishments—this meeting
feels it to be more than ever necessary that the
Society's friends should adhere with firmness
and with courage to their avowed principles,
whatever may be the difticu,tios or the temporary
disadvantages to which such a policy may expose
them.

Mr. Crum Ewing, M.P., moved, and Mr.
Neville Goodman of Cambridge, seconded the
last resolution, which was also carried unani-

mouely :
That recognising the value of the service ren-
dered to tilt) cause of religious equality by the
motion submitted to the House of Commons by

Mr. Miall last session, the meeting has pleasure in
learning that he is about again to bring the sub-
ject of disestablishment before Parliament, and
trusts that he will receive an increased degree of
both public and Parliamentary support.
A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded
the proceedings.

THE EARLY. CLOSING, ASSOCIATION

The annual meeting of the above association
was held on Tuesday night, at the Inns of
Court Hotel, Holborn, Mr. W. C. Jay, of
Regent-street, occupying the chair. Speaking
of his long connection with the movement, the
Chairman said it was extremely gratifying to
him to notice the progress it was making, and
the improvement which had been effected in
the condition of the class of assistants. Great
reforms had been introduced since a time
which be could recollect, when the usual hours
of labour were from six in the morning till
twelve at night, or sometimes one or two in
the morning. The amelioration of the condi-
tion of life had also been accompanied by an
elevation of the assistants' position, socially
and morally. Twenty years ago the vice of
drunkenness was a very prevalent one among
this hard-worked class. The few moments that
could be snatched from toil were usually spent
in the public-house. It was a mistake to
suppose, as many people did, that the assist-
ants would make a bad use of the increased
leisure afforded them. It was shown that.
there was a groat improvement in the young
men; drunkenness was quite an exception;
many of the assistants were men of excellent
attainments, and followed various pursuits,
which redounded very much to their credit—
notably, those of natural history and scientific
experiments with the microscope. Moreover,'
salaries had improved, as a better class of
assistants came into the trade, and a good man
could now earn treble the amount that was
formerly paid. The report read by Mr.
Walker, the secretary, stated that the receipts
and expenditure of the Association for the past
year have been over £l,OOO. In the early
closing on Saturdays, the shortening of the
hours on ordinary nights, and in reference to
the Bank Holidays Act as applied to assist-
ants, some very important advantages had
been obtained by the efforts of the Association.
Several leading firms in the south and east
districts of London had consented to close .
their establishments at 2 p.m. on Saturdays,
and also to shorten their ordinary hours of
labour, their example being followed by many
others in their respective neigbourhoods. The
Saturday Half-holiday Guide, which had
been issued, had sold very largely, and a new
edition in a different form was about to be
issued. While, however, the Association bad
been very successful in its endeavours with
regard to some branches of trade, especially
Manchester warehouses, the iron trade, &e.,
there were other branches in which, from the
peculiar circumstances surrounding them,
little or no improvement has been effected,
viz., the grocery, apparel, and provision
trades. The hours are still extremely late,
extending to ten, eleven, and sometimes oven
twelve o'clock at night. The obituary con-
tained the names of two gentlemen, Professor
Maurice and ML'. A. Schoolbred, who had.
both taken an interest in the movement, Pro-
'essor Maurice evecially, having been one

of the oldest friends of the- Association. The
report having been read. and adopted, several
gentlemen were re-elected to the board of
management on their retirement, and some
other business having been transacted, the
proceedings concluded with a gordial vote of:
thanks to the chairman.

BATUEDAY, MAY 4, 1872.

THE FARMER'S FRIENDS,

MARK PIMAVIPS on old manufacturer
who for many years rreprectented Manchester
In Parliament. He is now a landowner in
Warwickshire, and perhaps has a sucker in
each field of industry, enriching himself with
one from. the land, and with the other from the
succulent soil of commerce. It is not known
that
.110 over did any good tea living soul
whilst in Parliament, though he proved quite
demonstratively that to shorten the hours of

labour for factory children and women Would
ruin the commerce of the country. The inward
light by which he did this has been for a long
time hidden under a bushel in Warwickshire,
but it has again been revealed. The patriarch
has come forth to prove that 18s, per week for
agricultural labourers is an impossibility, and
that Mr, Anon and his followers who are
asking for some approach this unconscionable
sum, are most extravagant and unreason-
able in their, demands. In doing this
he has recited a catalogue of farmers'
losses as dreary and terrible as those poured in
the old days into the alarmed ear of JOB.
From 1868 to the present moment there has
scarcely been anything but failures of une
kind or other—first wheat, then oats, then
barley—then the sun came and burnt '
.up the
green crops, and scorched and, withered the
root crops—then the rains descended and
drowned the earth. The straw failed. The
sheep became lean rand would grow no good
fleeces, and the foot-and-mouth disease
followed as a crowning grief, and now worse
than all, comes Mr. ABM and his hungry
labourers, who will no doubt, if not checked,
swallow all the rest, leaving the farmers lean
as their sheep, withered as their crops,
exhausted and barren as their land which has
been so ill-treated during the last four years
by sun and rain.

This is a very bad state of things, but after
all, do they furnish sufficient reason why a
labourer should not get properly paid for
his work? Should HODGE be content
with his hunger because the sun and rain
will not conduct themselves properly, and
come and. go when the farmers want them?
When the farmer grumbled of these things
to the landlord, did that generous creature
with tears in his eyes tell the poor tenant to
put the rent back 'again into his pocket, go
home and make merry, in the hope of better
crops next year? Or .when the farmer took
his limited amount of hay, and straw, and
beef, and mutton, and wool to market, and
the purchaser giumbled at enhanced prices,
did the farmer, pitying his distress, drop the
price to meet his necessities? The farmer's
misfortunes were no doubt national losses;
but, did the Bishops or Clergy abate their
claims? Did cabinet-ministers lop their in..,
comes? Did lawyers reduce their fees? Or
did tradesmen voluntarily stint their profits.?
Did they not all, in fad, get whatever theywere
legally entitled to, and. in every way as much
as they could? We know of no code of good
nature that was set up to displace the old law
of supply and demand; no spontaneous effort
which caused the wealth of the well-to=do to
.flow out on the needy. In this inilleflial work
HoDOE is asked to set the' example, and starve
deaorouily with his &rail) in silence lest others
should have their comfort' interfered with.
The labourer is now isking for 15s per week.
Let us hope he will soon demand 18s, and
more, if it can begot. Remember, you dis-
ciples of the dismal science, his labour isrbis
cofilmoclity, it is the only thing he has to sell,
and be must get the best price he can for it.
His demands have been so far the least exact-
ing, and he has gained less by work and wages
than, any other member of the community.
Mr. MARK PHILLIPS once thought that if the
labour of women and little children was
abridged ruin would overtake the manufac-
turers. The abridgment was made and in-
creased prosperity, not ruin, fellowed. tot
him not croak and prophesy again. In the
commotion now on foot silence is his., duty.
We want peace, but we desire justice.

Lord, let the human, storm be atill'd !
Lord, lot the million mouths be filled !
Let labour cease to toil in vain!
Let Englond be herself again !

CONVOCATION-THE ATHANASIAN
CREED.

IT would be difficult to describe with aeou-
racy the character of the debates whieh took
place a few days since in both Howes of Con-
vocation on the propriety of reading the
Athenasian Creed to the congregations in our
churches. Whether this ought or ought not
to be done is a question raised by the clergy
themselves, What the meaning and effect of
it when done is a question also raised by the
clergy. Fortunately the matter is one whioh no
two sensible laymen would lose two minutes in

discussing. Humane, sensible men throughout
Europe have got quite beyond this, and with-
out any effort net originating in the Church,
the most manly and reasonable portions of
the clergy are seeking to follow them.
As a matter of course many will refuse to
move. They have been all their lives reading
the damuatory clauses of this creed, and either
from habit or natural inclination they would
miss what is very pleasant if they gave them
up, and these persons ought not to be hurried.
Now that swearing has become low and vulgar/
it cannot but be pleasant to be able to damn
our neighbours on high recognized authority.
Besides as nobody believes that any harm
comes of it, beyond the uncharitable and
generally had example set—it is really a mat-
ter of very little consequence whether it be
continued or dropped. What we learn from
the debate in Convocation is that a certain num-
ber of the bishops and their clergy are disposed
to be as reasonable and humane as other
people, prefer love to hatred, and would rather
not damn those committed, to their cearge. As
for the rest we can wait. Foolish people
will be foolish people to the end of the
world, and BONZES and LAMAS, as well as
country clergyman rre no exception to the
rule. Let ti 'n cursing, whilst the
rest of the work in charity,
.and per-
forms the daily duties iife in a kindly and
improving spirit; and it will be seen some
day which has been best employed; and from
which most good has come to the world.

CHURCH AND STATE IN PRUSSIA.

THE " rastoral " of the Prussian Catholic,
Bishops is a public challenge thrown down W.
the Government. These are the instructions
it gives to the clergy as to the inspection of
public schools :—" Every rector has to inspect'
in his own parish without special authorisa--.
tion. But such authorisation is necessary
when he is invited (by Government) to inspect
either county schools or parish schools- nob in
his parish. In .:case the clerical inspectors
should be invited to do anything in collision
with their ecclesiastical duties, they are not
to give up their Mace without consulting their
clerical superiors. The priest appointed as:
inspector is to communicate to his Bishop
every change concerning his position and
duties, and also the cancelling of his appoint-,
ment." From these instructions it is dear
that the Bishops consider every clergyman
appointed an inspector a man to be mistrusted,
and. will refuse consent to such appointments.
It will be seen how the clergy behave' when
acceptance of an appointment is forbidden by
the prelates. Will the Old Catholics have the
benefit of the struggle?

The Provincial Government of Vppor
Silesia, the centre of' the struggle, has urged.
the Landraths to give effect to the new legis-
lation. The Landraths are a kind of official
squirearchy. Government now calls upon,
them, who all look upon Prince Brouncx as
their prototype, to take upon themselves volun-
tarily the inspection of the parish schools in
their distriots, and thus overlook the inspector
as the inspector overlooks the schoolmaster.
The Government hopes the schoolmasters will
understand that the Landreth is to protect
them against their inspector, where he is a
Catholio clergyman. The Landraths are par-
ticularly to see that German is taught, and
are to draw up a list of such schoolmasters as
by their zeal against the Ultramontone clergy
deserve to be rewarded with grants of money.
The schoolmasters are reminded that, though,
as a rule, they are paid by the parish and not
by Government, except when the parish is too
poor, they are, nevertheless, Government
functionaries, subject to Government disci-
pline, and that Government cannot allow the*
to become members of
,Clubs or of Associations
intended to defeat the objects of the new law,
concerning the inspection of schools. The
struggle between Church and State in Prussia
assumes greater proportions daily, and ex-
tends from one branch of the public service to
another.

articles.title: UNIONISM AND STRIKE.
articles.text:
UNIONISM AND STRIKE.

TILE spirit of unionism is taking possession
of all seas of employed persons, carters, men-
servants, and maid-servants among the rest.
The "domestic*" of Dundee have set an
example which is sure to spread southwards.

In many' respects, no doubt, service in families
is very, comfortable, and it is paid for by
improving wages. But a large portion of
women servants are subjected to an endless
drudgery little removed from abject slavery.
The men-servants who met at Leamington
to discuss their grievances were told by their
chairman that their condition is "even worse
than that of slaves." They have formed a
union to comprise butlers and footmen, coach-
men and grooms, gardeners and porters. The
carters of Liverpool are on strike to the
number of two thousand, for increased wages,
shorter hours, and extra pay for overtime. It
is calculated that the strike has put a stop
to the work of five thousand dock labourers.
Many of the masters are described as driving
their own teams in silk hats. and kid gloves.
No collision has occurred between the men on
strike and those at work. A scheme to fill the
vacant places by means of men from Warwick-
stire seems to have utterly failed.

THE APPELLATE JURISDICTION OF
THE HOUSE OF LORDS.
LORD CAIRNS, with the countenance of
Lords WEsratrar and PENZANCE, has made
short work of the LORD CHANCELLOR'S Supreme
Court of Appeal Bill; which at his suggestion,
has been referred to a Select Committee, which
a to inquire into the working of the appellate
jurisdiction of the House, and into the work-
ing of the system of appeals to her Majesty in
Council, and whether any, and what improve-
ments should be made therein. Lord
CAIRNS, in the course of an elaborate attack
on the Bill, said, that last year there was a
great desire in some quarters to abolish the
House of Lords altogether, and the Prime
Minister, referring to it in a celebrated
speech, said, that,before he consented to any-
thing of the sort, ho should be tempted to
think once, twice, or even three times. Ho
(LORD C4IRNS) doubted whether that state-
ment held. out any great security for the
Rouse of Lords, and the construction put on
the present proposal would be, that it was an
important step towards the abolition of the
House as soon as the NIUE MINISTER had had
leisure to think the requisite number of times.
At the Same time, said Lord WESTBURY, their
Lordshipsmust not delude themselves with the
notion that their appellate jurisdiction could
remain as it was. If anything would
strengthen their Lordships' House, it would be
showing themselves [ready to make the fact
accord with the theory. The LORD CHAN-
cELLog, likewise repeated again, in defiance of
Lord CAralis, that their Lordships had never
as a House attempted, since 1780, to exercise
the ,j urisdietion in question. Indeed, if they
were to do so, their appellate functions would
not last for three weeks. Earl GRA.NVILLE,
referring to what Lord CAIRNS had said
respecting the inference drawn out of doors
with regard to the effect of the Bill upon the
permanence of their Lordships' House, said he
hadnot met with a single expression of that kind
In the press. Lord CAIRNS said he would take
care the noble EA.RL was put in full possession
of the expressions to which he had referred.

THE CARLIST RISING IN SPAIN.
Tux accounts from Spain are various, not
to say contradictory. Probably, however, the
Carlist rising will be easily put down. There
is at present no strong reason for believing
that the Republicans will join the Legitimists.
Of course, those parties are mutually repellent.
The presence of DON CARLOS on Spanish soil
is, not ascertained, though, in a proclamation
to "Spaniards, " signed your "King, CAnxos,"
lie "thanks GOD for permitting him to kiss
the soil of his country," It is not hard to
guess who wrote a document in which it is
asserted that the holy'religion of our fathom is
persecuted." Indeed, it is explicitly stated
that every Carlist band in the field has a priest
either at its head or as second in command.
The acceptance by a well-known. Radical of
the COIDDIaIIa of a column of soldiers under
Marshal SERRANO is one evidence of the
loyalty of the party to the Crown and Consti-
tution, We read of some bands as defeated
and dispersed, and of others as avoiding de-
feat by submission. DON CkuLos speaks of
dying for his people if he cannot save them,
but it is to be hoped he will not "kiss the
sacred soil" in that sense of the expression.

RELIGIOUS TENDENCIES ON THE
CONTINENT.

NEITTIER the "Old Catholics" of Germany,
nor the independent Gallicans in France
appear to pay much heed to the mock
thunders from Rome against them. Dr.

DOLLINGER is in close communication with
Anglican dignitaries who sigh after a Catho-
licism denounced by Pope and Cardinals, and
the Abbe JIINQUA is lecturing in conventual
chapels at Brussels against the decrees of Pius
and the Council. Our Bishop of ELY, how-
ever, and our Bishop of LINCOLN, though near
neighbours in point of diocese, evidently con-
template those French and German movements
from different points of view. Although the
latter, at a meeting of the Anglo-Continental
Society, moved a resolution of sympathy with
DOLLINGER and his compatriot associates, he
was unable to conceal his misgivings as to
the results of the agitation. According
to his motion there are the liveliest hopes for
the future of the Austrian Church growing
out of the present upstir ; but, according to
his speech, members of free political Govern-
ments arc quailing under the frowns and ful-
minations of the Vatican, against which, as
his lordship sees matters, they have nothing
to sot but a spirit of socialism. Nay, Dr.
Wonnswount avows his persuasion, that, in a
short time, even we, notwithstanding the sea
which surrounds us, with whatever checks
and safeguards such a circumstance may inter-
pose, may be caused to shiver before the
mighty power of the Infallible Old Gentleman,
unless we do something to destroy it, By
what means, we should like to know, does the
mere ecclesiastic, himself enthroned in Lin-
coln Minster, propose to bring about that
destruction? For our ownpart, we know of no
resources on which the See of Rome can now fall
back at all more palpable or stronger than
the zeal of the clergy who serve under it.
Perhaps, indeed, Dr. WORDSWORTH has con-
vinced himself that DON CIRLOS will
dethrone KING AIIADEUS, M. TIMMS 011t-
manceuvro PRINCE Bismutcr, and something
happen to turn out VICTOR EMANUEL from 010
Quirinal Palace. If the Papacy has no
better hopes than these, woo be to it! As
for English Churchmen, if they mean to
neutralise the efforts of Jesuit intriguers, it
must not be attempted by striving to beat
them at their own weapons, but by a scheme
of defensive operations as diametrically opposite
as ingenuity can devise.
We observe, however, that the Bishop of
LINCOLN argues the point on the assumption
of the POPE'S loss of temporal power being a
great gain to His Holiness. That the Church to

;14110h-hill Lordship belongs might be a gainer
through separation from the State, we have
DO doubt at all. Bat it sets up no pretensions
to spiritual domination like the Church of

Rome. The POPE aud Conclave might be re-

&teed as to temporal possessions to that more
needle's point on which, according to the old
casuist all the angelic host of heaven could
dance together; but they would not on that
account lot go the claim to power over all
consciences, which is the fundamental idea of
this religious scheme. It is by denying this
they are to be encountered and over-mastered;
and of denying it with practical efficiency
there is no other method open than that of
contending for the fullest liberty of conscience
on the ground of every man's indivivual per-
sonal accent) tableness to his Maker for the
use ho makes of his human faculties.
The Bishop of ELY talks in a different style.
Ho pleads for unity, as consistent with truth.
But, as PILATB asked, what is truth?
We do not 'repeat the question mockingly.
Truth, in Churchmen's sense of the word, is
" orthodoxy ;" but, according to the old story,
many men have a doxy of their own, not easily
harmonised with the dray of another. It
seems, however, that the reaction produced by
the proclamation of the dogma of infallibility
and by other causes, is expressing itself in a
desire to find out that form of Protestantism
with which the new protesters may best ally
themselves. The American bishops who have
lately visited our shores assured Dr. HA.ROLD
BROWN and other Anglicans, that they very
much like the Church of England, and they
also told them that, not in Italy only but even
in the East, American clergymen on their

travels bear witness to a strong feeling for
closer alliance with the Anglican com-
munion. The Archbishop of SYlt.t, who
was a while ego among us, professes
a desire for a perfect 'union, and
sets the Old. Catholics of Germany
as no less than the English clergy moved by

the spirit of evangelical truth in contrast with
"the impious dogma brought forward by
sinful men." The old Oriental, nevertheless,
is terribly afraid Jest DOLLINGER and the rest
should overstep the bounds within which they
ought to limit their efforts. Yet we cannot
perceive in the tone of that learned leader's
correspondence with Englishmen, anything to
cause alarm in an enlightened mind. He
seems to be feeling after new foundations
having abandoned thcse on which till lately his
beliefs were supposed to rest. He says,
indeed, too little about Holy Scripture and too
much about the writings of divines of this
school or of that; but, if he is either Ration-
alist or Socialist in his tendencies, he does not
allow the fact to be seen.

The Bishop of ELY, from his point, lets us see
some way into his mind, and the speculations
in which these continental stirrings engage it.
We must not, his Lordship intimates, forget
that all these movements are tending to the
disintegration of the ancient Churches on the
Continent, with an impossibility of telling what
the coming together of the atoms again may
be. The natural gravitation of the disinte-
grated atoms is not, he is afraid, towards
truth, but rather towards unbelief. The great
danger of all these movements is, n9t that they
will issue finally in the reformation of the
Churches of the Continent, but that in many

instances they will result in the shaking of the
faith of large numbers of persons, and in turn-
ing them over, not to any form of sound belief,
but to some of the various forms of rationalism
which are bidding at the present moment for
the custom of Christians in Europe.
We will not take upon ourselves to say either
yea or nay to such speculations as these. Well,
however, would it be for those churches of
Christendom that are not immediately threat-
ened with schism, division, and "disintegra-
tion," to take warning in time, and look to it
that their preaching and teaching, profession
and practice, be such as to accord closely with
the sayings and doings of CHRIST, whom
they avow as their master and model. It is
the assumption of ecclesiastical power and its
overstrained exertion that have brought certain
Churches into disrepute, and now menace them
with destruction. Let Churchmen, of whatso-
ever name, realise in their own behaviour that
sketch of Christianity which we gave two
weeks ago in the words of Abbe JITNQUA ; and
the Bishops of LINCOLN and ELY would have
little occasion to dread any violent or perilous
recoil towards either socialism or unbelief.

articles.title: NEW PARTY.
articles.text:
A NEW PARTY.

• TnosE who understand best the mechanism
of political combinations hint at a possible
arrangement whereby a new party may
constitute itself almost immediately. It is
believed that the present Liberal party in Parlia-
ment, or rather the Ministry and its imme-
diate friends, are nearly played out. They
have done all they wish to do, and desire a
rest, which will not be granted so long as they
remain in power. There can be no doubt
whatever that this is the feeling of the Old
Whigs. They have been made the instru-
ments for doing more than ever they intended,
and would be glad of any fair opportunity to
turn their backs on those of their party
who have not become tired yet of seeking
the improvements of the nation by decided
changes in the constitution. By themselves,
however, this section of the Liberal party be-
comes every day less influential. And to join
with the Conservatives whilst their own party
remains in power would be regarded and
punished by the country as a treason.
• It is not, however, unlikely that at the next
election the Conservative party will obtain a
considerable accession of strength in the
House of Commons. Its old chiefs will most
likely be installed in power, and a truce may
be patched up between them and the most
timid and hesitative of our old Liberals
which may lead to the solidifying of a kind of
middieparty, wiliph, if, it works clgilitooY

a practical way on small measures of imme-
diate utility, may manage to retain power for
a considerable time. There are many indica-
tions that something like this may be looked
for. It is almost certaiu that if a dozen or
two leading men set seriously about the con-
struction of such. a, party, and could agree
amongst themselveS as to, a fair division,of
the spoils of office, and the apportionment of
political influence, that. a scheme might be
easily enough carried into. effeJt.
Everything will, of course, depend on

_
the attitude of the working people. At present
both parties seek to maintain themselves by
courting the working people; Mr. GLADSTONE
at one moment makes a bid, and Mr. DrsnaEra
at another. But this game has gone on as
far as it can safely be carried. Every new
advance in popular concession frightens the
timid of both parties, and what these men
sigh for above all things is such a junction of
their forces as would enable them to resist all
further popular demands. What has been
done already frightens them, what may be
done alarms them still more. Widening of
the franchise, Ballot Bills, Altering of land
tenure, Education Bills,. Irish Church destruc-
tion, and Agricultural labourers' movements
at home—threatened Republican action abroad
—lnternational mysteries darkly hinted at in
the Press, fill them with vague fears, seas
almost necessarily to create in them the.dosire,
by union amongst themselves, to balance and
neutralise popular action.
The state of things amongst the working
people is such as to give encouragement to
such a design. There is really no bond of
union amongst the working men of England.
There is no determined well-defined thought
as to any necessary work; no clear concep-
tion of any principle entertained in co mmon
by them. They originate nothing; have no
hearty faith in any understood policy. Their
thoughts on labour questions are expressed
solely by their trades unions which are non-
political. Their ideas in connection with the
great pauper question have neither form nor
colour. They have little or no influence in
the eleotione of the country because they have
no dominant ideas, and no organisation of
value. If they were sufficiently trained
politically, a common faith in common ideas
would give thorn immense power in influencing
the policy of the nation,, and in determining
the direction of its living active forces.
Whether this third or middle party will be able
to constitute itself and seek and obtain power it
would be premature to say; but that the
present Liberal party, by its want of courage
and consistent action ; and the working
people, by their indifference and want of pur-
pose, have opened for them the opportunity to
do so, there can be no doubt.

your journal of last weak I was

dom I.know there are rules of the

We should in bringing about that which is

ciety would have to be thrown in Chancery and ,

scribe towards my expenses if I went to law.

THE CLEVEIAND MINERS
To the Editor, of the BEE-Ilivr.
Si a,—We, the Miners of Cleveland, have long
been halting between two opinions ; for'we have
long been taught to believe by our sympathetic
employers that trade unions are detrimental
to a happy and an industrious people, whose
felicity is unequalled by any other nation in
the world. Therefore, it is evidently stated
by our eniployeri that, were we to form our-
selves into a united body, we should, at all
events, tring ourselves, our wives, and our
little ones to ' absolute penury. Therefore,
whosoever is deceived by joining the union
is not wise, and is culpably blameable for
driving our trade from our midst. .sllt,
however, be that as it may, we are yet some-
what desirous to know how it is that the
South and West k orkshire coalminers suffer
no more through the depression of trade than
we do although they are one of the beat
•
organised bodies in the whole universe, and
arc, at this moment, receiving a higher re-
muneration for their labour than any other
miners in Great Britain, This certainly
Proves they derive their, benefits from their
united action. There have been many attempts
made to unite the Cleveland miners, but up to
the present all such attempts have been made
in vain. Therefore it As evident to one and
all in the Cleveland district, that in 1807-8
we had to work only four days a week for a
considerable time, and, as there was no,union
in this district at that period, it was utterly
impossible for the iron trade to be affected by our
united action as we had now, although we at
that period suffered worse than any of the united
districts, yet our avaricious taskmasters would
fain make us believe that our position i 3
second to none as a mining, population. lam
therefore instructed to say on behalf of my
fellow-workmen that we thank them for their
advice, but can't accept of it as we do not con-
sider it worth six, and eightpence; and there-
fore declined to listen do any more of their
infernal and hellish twaddle whioli has so
long governed a credulous aud down-trodden
race of people. nut the year 1872 is the new
epoch for the Cleicland miners, for we have
formed ourselves into an organisation, and we
have fetched our foundation stone from, the
South and West Yorkshire district, and on.
Thursday, the 28th of March, the first founda-
tion stone was laid and the Miners' Distriot
Council built thereon' with its eight hundred
members 23 pillars to support the mighty
fabric and several local lodges, will form the
steps to the miners' chamber. of council. On
Monday, April the Bth,' the first delegate
meeting will be held at Bratton in the noted
Star Chamber. The name of the association
is tke North Yorkshire Cleveland Miners'
Association, and is making rapid progress in
the onward march of reform. It is initiating
from 50-to 100 members weekly.
Therefore, the miners of Cleveland are
snaking arrangements with Mr. M'Donald, for
joining the Miners' National Association, and
will, therefore, be represented at the first Con,
ferenoeoonvened by the Miners' National Coun-
oil, and if, as. Mr. McDonald informs me, the
conference will be held in the north of Eng-
land, then there will be a public Demonstra
tion with the Cleveland miners either at the
beginning or at the end of the conference sit-
ting in order that the miners of this district
may have the benefit of being addressed by
the leading meinbers of the council. Then
-again, sir, we know perfectly well that we have
never had an advance in our wages equivalent
to the well-organised districts, in fact these
lordly stone kings evade every lavr of humanity
and ride rough shod over the Governmental
laws of our country, and laugh to scorn at them
,with impunity; for Instance, here may be seen

enginemen, and when I say enginemen, I
mean the very men who have charge of the
winding engines; yes and these inconsiderable
wretches may be seen reading newspapers,
novels, and comic song books, at the time they
are raising or lowering the miners too or from
the mines, and on the 26th inst., one of these
illiterate fellows was seen perusing his
favourite Hamlet, "I am thy father's ghost,"
who must have imagined this well-know ap-
parition was there in reality, for he lost all
power of himself and all control of the en-
gine. Thus the miners in the cage came rush-
ing between earth and sky with the velocity
of a thunder bolt, but thanks he to the
mighty hand of Providence, for the men had
the presence of mind to jump when going up
to the pulley wheels, some falling upon the
top of' the pit cabin' and the others on different
parts of the pit's top, and thus saved their
lives. Then; again, the same person did,
within a comparative short time since, lot the
cage and its cargo of human machines go with
considerable force to the pit's bottom, and by
so doing laid one man off-his work for seven-
teen weeks, and also gave the remainder a
terrible shock; and although the before men-
tioned miner was living in one of the com-
pany's houses, and was lamed through the
carelessness of an ignorant and insignificant
engine driver, yet notwithstanding all this
they laugh at it with impunity, for we have
invariably informed our employers of these
dangerous events, which so frequently take
place through the incompetency of such
illiterate fools, yet they have always turned a
deaf ear to the entreaties of their miner,
therefore it is evident that if we get no other
benefit from the Miners' National Association
we aliall certainly have our lives protected, and
yet our employers andtheir demagogues would
have us believe there is no benefit in union.
Surely if the Miners National Council steps in
and enforces the right of law and saves the
men from being smashed to pieces at the
pit'a bottom, surely this will be a benefit to the
miners, if it is not the masters; then again,
miners of Cleveland, I have recommended
the 13Ex-IlivE to you as a journal that will
faithfully, represent You, for I have been con.

breath of life and therefore can vouch for its
integrity; and as you have already adopted it
as your organ, I shall expect you to fulfil
your promise, for remember he that is faithful
in little is expected to be faithful in
I am, yours truly,

THE POSITION OF THE BALLOT
QUESTION.
To the Editor of the BEE-Him
Sin,—The advocates of secret voting must not
be di scoura ged by the rejection of Mr. Le atham'
amendment. The adoption of that ameud-
ment might have made "assurance doubly
sure," and Mr: Leathern is entitled to praise
for his desire to prevent all doubt as to the
vote being given in secrecy; but it must be
remembered that the Bill of the Government
was framed for the same purpose, and the
provisions of that Bill may, after all, be
sufficient for its accomplishment. Let us look
at some of those provisions. Clause 2 pro-
vides that the voter shall mark his ballot paper
secretly, and fold it up "so as to conceal his
vote.' Clause 4 provides "that every officer,
clerk, and agent," at a ptilling station "shall
maintain, and aid in maintaining, the secrecy
of the voting," shall not "attempt to obtain ''
or " communicate " information as to the way
in which any elector "is about to vote or has
voted," and shall not, directly or indirectly,
induce any elector to display his ballot paper,"
so as to make known he has voted. The
penalty for acting in contravention of these,
provisions is "imprisonment for any term net
exceeding three months, with or without hard
labour.' The 19th clause of the first
schedule directs the presiding officer to 'e
elude all persons except the voters, and "the
clerks, agents, and constables on duty."
The 'lst clause of the same schedule prO-
vides that "every officer, clerk, or ngent
authorised to attail at a polling station shall,
before the oneninrof the poll, make a MAW-
tory declaration of secrecy." 4 iThe form of
directions an to voting, at the end of'the
second Schedule, instructs the voter to "fold
up the ballot Taper" before he leaves the
compartment in which he has marked it, and
put it into the ballot-box " witheut showing
the front of the paper to any person." Clause
14 in Schedule 1 provides for the furnishing
of compartments "in which the voters can
mark their votes screened from observation."
I think a careful consideration of these provi-
sions will satisfy the friends of the Ballot, that
the Government is sincere in its expressed
desire to protect the secrecy of the vote, and
that it would be very difficult for a few corrupt
or cantankerous persons to destroy that
secrecy; and the public feeling of the country
against law-breakers of every description
would very soon brand such persons with
deserved obliquy. J. F. BONTEMS,

laws of barter and exchange. The enormous
profits which the middle classes have recently,
realised by the sudden rise in the price of
everything, from a horse-shoe nail to a landed
estate, naturally contribute to confirm the
working men in. their serious error; and as so
many common people, of little learning and
less judgment, have shared in the benefit of
this commercial windfall, the operatives are
all the less able to perceive why they
alone should be excluded from the bless-
ings of Such ft prosperous time when
men not much above them are enjoying it all
to their fill. Considering their defective
education, we cannot blame them for ignoring
that whatever the origin and poeition of :4
man, if he has managed to save something and
invest it in business or stock, he is entitled to
profit by certain chances necessarily closed
against the proletariat who lives from hand to
mouth; nor can they be held responsible for
disregarding the fact that if the vast develop-
ment of trade has enriched the owners of eiery
variety of goods, speculation has done a great
deal to aid' the process, and has created ficti-
tious. values,. pro tem., which may turn out
to be' nothing at all, and inflict infinite-loss
upon the last holder. In all these important
points the ignorance of our operatives has
been turned to good account by the socialistic
members of thustrike Committees. .The whole
tone of the labouring community indicates
this. The men begin to doubt the fairness of
the existing state of things. They theorize in
their own crude way about the division of
profits, and profess the most sanguine hores
as to the Mitre prospects of their order.
Although revolutionary ideas are nowhere
broached, except in the few small conventicles
of avowed Communists, there is
.yet a
lurking tendency to question the Justice
of arrangements which humanity has so
long considered indispensable. The labour-
ing man does not -menace, but he de-
mands; he does not' dream dream of using vio-
lence, but he is confident that he will some
how or other be enabled to effect a radical
change in the time-honoured ini3titutions of
society. This revulsion in the opinion of the
men is the more remarkable because there
exists in this country a large number of
masters in a small way, who are scarcely any
better off than their hands. This class, whose
only distinguishing feature consists in possess-
ing tools and a workshop of their own, has
always been very numerous in 17, race who4e
ideal is persotal independence. Until a short
time ago, these *mall masters constituted a.
connecting link between the more wealthy em-
ployers and the labouring men.'. But they
have ceased to do so, and are either ranked with
the artisans or with the "bloated bourgeois."
If very pbor, they make common cause with
the ordinary labourer; if a little above the
level of the masses, they try, to resist the en-
eroaohments of the "geselle, ' and fight their
oWn battle as sturdily as-those on the highest
rbund of the ladder, r.the artisans at present
know only allies or enemies, and so the small
master must make their choice. Such is the
separating effect of the war of classes in its
veryiontset.
All these marked social and commercial
innovations could not help producing ulterior
results. The year 1872 had scarcely opened
when masters began to prepare more zealously
than ever for the redoubled activity, which in
this cold climate comes in with the summer.
Immediately, the Berlin building trades turned
recusant. Itementbering late defeats, the
masters this time thought discretion the better
part of valour, and gave in without a struggle.
Before a strike could be organised, the masons
and carpenters of the metropolis succeeded in
obtaining 3s. 9d. and 10 hours, instead of the
3s. 6d. and 11 hours accordei them in the
past year. Good workmen had. even 4s. 64,
conceded them, a very fair rate of remunera-
tion, especially when it is taken into account
that two hours for luncheon, dinner, and
coffee must be deducted from the stipulated
ten. Is not nearly £7O a year enough for a
