tradesiben, with 384,783 workmen under them. By 1861,
notwithstanding the havoc worked ,by the progress of
wholesale manufacture, the total of the masters had
increased to 550,324, and that of the workmen to 542,044.
The population during the sarne period increased from 171
millions to 181 millions. But the last ten years, when the
roanufacturing movement has given an inkling of its
comin, g omnipotence, are believed to have produced a much
tar4er addition to the number 01 the workmen than to that
4:4 the masters.

mason, when an assidttane judge, after serving
five years unsalaried, is, in the sixth year of
his public career) blessed with the magnificent
salary of Xl6O ? The carpenters think other-
wise. Encouraged by their fresh success, they
have just struck in a body, deliaanding that the
4s. fid, which hitherto constituted the earn-
ings of skilled hands should be conceded
to all indiscriminately. Another point they
insist upon is a fortnight's notice before
dismissal. With the free and independent
manna rs now-in days prevailing among the
men, Masters have no other means of making
them do their duty but instantaneous dismissal
as hitherto practised. However, notwithstand-
ing the firmness with which the masters stand
their ground, the masons begin to imitate the
example of the carpenters, and betray a diss
position likewise to organise a general strike
with the same programme. The cigarmakers
have also left their factories, asking for
similar terms ; and as the three trades men-
tioned are the most enterprising of all and
generally take the lead in the movements of
the labouring classes, the sligbest success of
one Will be the signal for the resumption of
last year's general campaign, and bring the
entire working community into the field.
Already in Rhineland the tilecutters, knife-
grinders and other workers in iron are begin-
ning active operations. At Kiel masons and
carpenters have hoisted the fiag of oppposition,
and at Chemnitz the attitede of the engine-
makers is so disquieting that the masters have
entered into a league for common defence, and
asked. their colleagues throughout Germany
to join them.. There is reason to believe that
similar precautions have been taken by the
men of all the different trades, and that for
the present at any rate the organization of the
artisans is more comprehensive and strict than
that of the masters. It is terrible to contem-
plate what the upshot of this social warfare
would be, were it to continue long enough to
see the greater part of masters and men arrayed
in two hostile and well-disciplined camps.
Thus far the police have had but little
extra work on account of the strikes.
Although an unpleasant feeling predominates
among the lower classes, acts of violence are
rare. Even in the larger towns, where the
men have been most worked upon by the Social-
ists, those actually convinced of the justice of
these sanguine speculations are far too few to
attempt to proceed from words to blows.
There is, too, something in the refleetive and
temperate turn of the national character
which makes the very victims of Socialist
delusions doubt the honesty and practicability
of the charming visions they see in their
pharitasmagorian creed. Asa rule, the men,
though regarding the masters as competitors,
and opposing them with all the weapons fair
in commercial rivalry, do not hate them.
They are intent upon curtailing the masters'
profits to their own advantage, and. bitterly
resent every allusion to their former subordi-
nate state ; but they are still equitable enough
to distinguish between social opposition and
personal enmity, and shrink from bestow-
ing elegant appellatives upon those whom
they do not mind calling their ad-
versaries. In this respect the German
artisan in differs as yet moat satisfactorily
from his French comrade. A. few isolated
instances excepted, our operatives have ab-
stained from all excess during the whole
exciting period of last year's strikes: In the
few cases wherein official interference was
called for, the executive authorities made
short work with.the offenders, and. the Courts
pronounced severe sentences upon them. In
Berlin, for instance, four and six months'
imprisonment were repeatedly awarded to men
who had attacked those who, would not join
the strike. Workmen who After undertaking
piece work made common cause with the rest,
were instantly imprisoned for breach of con-
tract, and only released. on promising that they
would fulfil their engagements.
(There is, hoWever, no denying that'he
temper of the men has become more irritable
than it was, and that society is looking for-
ward with dismay to the fresh troubles that
seem to be drawing on apace. Pending the
outburst; the scholarly mind of Germany is
attempting with fiery energy to grapple with
the-now question that has so suddenly gained
an unexpected importance in the country.
Nor arc practical philanthropists wanting to
allay the acrimony of the strife, and to try by
practical experiments to effect a reconciliation
between the contending parties. Of theii
meritorious efforts I hope to be able to speak
shortly.
